summary.one_liner: A curated collection of architecture decision record (ADR) templates, examples, guidance, and related tools for documenting significant software architecture decisions.
summary.what_it_does: The README explains what an ADR is and related terms (architecture decision log, architecturally-significant requirement) and gives practical advice on starting to use ADRs with teams, git, or other tools. It links to roughly a dozen ADR templates, including those by Michael Nygard, Jeff Tyree and Art Akerman, arc42, MADR, and Planguage, plus examples such as CSS framework, secrets storage, and monorepo vs multirepo decisions. It covers file naming conventions, tips for writing good Context and Consequences sections, and teamwork questions about who can create ADRs and how their lifecycle is governed. It also touches on architecture views and viewpoints, fitness functions for decisions as code, and PR guardrails such as ADR Guard. The repo ships two Claude Code skills under skills/ for writing ADRs, and the README lists translations into many languages.
use_cases: writing architecture decision records for a team
documenting why a technical choice was made
enforcing architecture decisions in pull requests
reviewing example decisions such as secrets storage or timestamp formats
how_to_run: Commit the ADR file to your git repo
To use the bundled Claude Code skills: copy a skill folder from skills/ into .claude/skills/ in your repository
notable: Collection of more than a dozen ADR templates from different sources, compared in the README
Teamwork guidance on who creates ADRs, lifecycle stages, and governance questions
Covers fitness functions and ArchUnit for checking decisions in code
Lists ADR tooling such as ADR Guard, Decision Guardian, and command-line tools
caveats: The README is a reference collection rather than a runnable tool; no installation is required beyond creating files
The README warns to do your own due diligence on linked resources before using them in critical systems
Some listed tools are third-party projects and are described only briefly
keywords: record why we chose a technology
